item.content:encoded:
The Kunming Biodiversity Fund 2026 Call for Proposals is inviting ambitious biodiversity projects designed to help developing countries protect ecosystems, integrate biodiversity into public policy, mobilize financial resources for conservation, and ensure the fair sharing of benefits arising from genetic resources.

Through this international funding opportunity, eligible country-level projects can request up to US$500,000, while regional projects involving multiple countries can receive up to US$800,000. Projects must run for a period of between 12 and 24 months and directly support implementation of the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework and relevant National Biodiversity Strategies and Action Plans.

The call is particularly relevant to governments, participating United Nations organizations and their implementing partners working to reverse biodiversity loss through practical, country-owned and scalable interventions. The engagement of Indigenous Peoples and Local Communities, women and young people is strongly encouraged throughout project design and implementation.

The first submission deadline is 15 September 2026, while the second submission deadline is 15 November 2026. Full details are available through the official UNEP announcement.

Kunming Biodiversity Fund 2026 Call for Proposals at a Glance

Key information Details
Fund Kunming Biodiversity Fund
Main purpose Accelerate implementation of national biodiversity priorities and the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework
Maximum amount for a single-country project US$500,000
Maximum amount for a multi-country project US$800,000
Project duration 12 to 24 months
Geographic scope Country-level, subnational or regional multi-country implementation
Stage 1 deadline 15 September 2026
Stage 2 deadline 15 November 2026
Submission time No later than 23:59 on the relevant deadline date
Submission method Email submission to the Kunming Biodiversity Fund Secretariat
Submission email kbf@un.org
Expected Stage 2 results By 31 December 2026
Programme support-cost ceiling No more than 7% for the participating UN organization

The announcement does not specify the applicable time zone for the 23:59 deadline. Applicants should therefore submit well before the closing day and request confirmation that the email and all attachments have been received.

What Is the Kunming Biodiversity Fund?

The Kunming Biodiversity Fund, commonly known as the KBF, is an international biodiversity financing and cooperation mechanism initiated and financially supported by the Government of China in strategic partnership with the United Nations Environment Programme.

The Fund was formally launched in Beijing in May 2024 to assist developing countries in accelerating and expanding the implementation of their National Biodiversity Strategies and Action Plans. It is intended to connect the global commitments made under the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework with practical conservation delivery at country and community levels.

The Fund mobilizes resources for biodiversity initiatives that are expected to be high-impact, inclusive and equitable. It also aims to complement existing biodiversity financing instruments, including the Global Biodiversity Framework Fund, while working closely with the Secretariat of the Convention on Biological Diversity and other United Nations organizations.

More information about the Fund’s background and institutional arrangements is available on the official Kunming Biodiversity Fund overview page.

Why Has the 2026 Call for Proposals Been Launched?

The Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework was adopted by the Parties to the Convention on Biological Diversity in 2022. Since then, countries and other stakeholders have taken steps to translate its global goals and targets into national action.

Governments have established national targets and expanded their efforts in areas such as biodiversity finance, institutional capacity, technology transfer, monitoring and scientific cooperation. Nevertheless, the global review of implementation indicates that progress is still not occurring at the scale or speed required to halt and reverse biodiversity loss.

Important implementation gaps remain, including:

  • Weak environmental governance and insufficient policy coordination;
  • Limited integration of biodiversity across government departments and economic sectors;
  • Inadequate whole-of-government and whole-of-society participation;
  • Shortages of biodiversity information, monitoring systems and technical capacity;
  • Insufficient financial resources for implementing national biodiversity plans;
  • Implementation bottlenecks affecting the delivery of national targets;
  • Limited participation and ownership among communities and other affected groups; and
  • A lack of scalable and replicable biodiversity interventions.

The 2026 call seeks proposals that address the root causes of these gaps and finance practical interventions capable of accelerating National Biodiversity Strategies and Action Plans.

Projects should be based on national circumstances and priorities rather than presenting generic conservation ideas without a clear connection to the beneficiary country’s biodiversity strategy.

Four Priority Thematic Areas

Every proposed project must contribute to at least one of the following four thematic areas. Projects that make a credible contribution to more than one area will be viewed favourably.

1. Restoring and Protecting Ecosystems to Improve Biodiversity and Ecosystem Services

The first thematic area supports projects that restore degraded ecosystems, strengthen ecosystem protection and improve the services that healthy ecosystems provide to people and nature.

Potential interventions may include:

  • Assessing the condition, extent, integrity and threats facing inland water, coastal and marine ecosystems;
  • Improving the protection and effective management of inland waters, coastal areas and marine environments;
  • Developing pilot projects for restoring degraded terrestrial, freshwater, coastal or marine ecosystems;
  • Recovering important ecosystem functions and services;
  • Strengthening biodiversity monitoring and ecosystem assessment systems;
  • Improving biodiversity information and data-management capabilities;
  • Evaluating the environmental and socioeconomic effectiveness of previous restoration initiatives;
  • Comparing the costs, adaptability and sustainability of different restoration approaches; and
  • Producing models that can be replicated or scaled in other locations.

Projects under this theme should demonstrate how restoration or protection activities will contribute to measurable biodiversity outcomes rather than concentrating only on infrastructure, awareness or short-term activities.

2. Mainstreaming Biodiversity into Policies, Regulations, Planning and Strategies

The second thematic area focuses on integrating biodiversity considerations into public policy, legislation, planning systems, development processes and economic decision-making.

Relevant activities may include:

  • Integrating biodiversity values into national and subnational policies;
  • Strengthening biodiversity provisions within laws, regulations and sectoral strategies;
  • Incorporating biodiversity into spatial and land-use planning;
  • Integrating biodiversity into poverty-reduction and development strategies;
  • Improving strategic environmental assessments and environmental impact assessments;
  • Reflecting biodiversity and ecosystem values in national accounting systems;
  • Mainstreaming biodiversity across agriculture, aquaculture, fisheries, forestry, energy, chemicals, mining, health, medicine and tourism;
  • Supporting fishing moratoriums, coastal wetland protection or sustainable fishing quotas;
  • Monitoring and reducing the excessive use of fertilizers and pesticides;
  • Promoting the efficient and responsible use of agricultural inputs;
  • Expanding biodiversity-friendly farming, agroecological approaches and agroforestry;
  • Monitoring soil health and pollinator populations; and
  • Improving coordination between public institutions whose decisions affect biodiversity.

Strong proposals should clearly identify the relevant policies, departments, sectors and decision-making processes that the project intends to influence.

3. Strengthening Resource Mobilization for Biodiversity Conservation

The third thematic area addresses the financial gap affecting the implementation of national biodiversity strategies.

Projects may focus on:

  • Identifying incentives and subsidies that are harmful to biodiversity;
  • Designing fair approaches for eliminating, reforming or phasing out harmful incentives;
  • Developing policies that encourage businesses to assess and disclose their biodiversity-related impacts, risks and dependencies;
  • Supporting companies in reducing the negative biodiversity effects of their operations, supply chains and production systems;
  • Developing or implementing national biodiversity finance plans;
  • Establishing payments for ecosystem services;
  • Developing green bonds and other nature-related financial instruments;
  • Designing biodiversity compensation, credit or benefit-sharing mechanisms;
  • Mobilizing domestic public-sector finance;
  • Attracting private-sector investment into biodiversity;
  • Using blended finance or impact-investment approaches;
  • Improving the transparency and effectiveness of biodiversity expenditure; and
  • Mobilizing international and domestic resources for National Biodiversity Strategies and Action Plans.

Projects should demonstrate how proposed financing mechanisms will become operational and sustainable. A proposal limited to conducting studies without a credible route to implementation may be less competitive.

4. Sharing Benefits from Genetic Resources and Digital Sequence Information

The fourth thematic area supports fair and equitable sharing of benefits arising from genetic resources, digital sequence information associated with genetic resources, and related traditional knowledge.

Relevant interventions may include:

  • Developing legal and policy measures for access and benefit-sharing;
  • Strengthening national, subnational and local administrative systems;
  • Building institutional and technical capacity;
  • Improving procedures governing access to genetic resources;
  • Protecting traditional knowledge associated with genetic resources;
  • Developing fair mechanisms for distributing monetary and non-monetary benefits;
  • Supporting compliance with relevant international access and benefit-sharing instruments; and
  • Piloting practical arrangements for access to and benefit-sharing from genetic resources, digital sequence information and traditional knowledge.

Projects in this area should give careful attention to community rights, informed participation, transparency and the ownership of traditional knowledge.

The detailed scope of all four areas is explained in the 2026 Full Size Project Application Guidelines.

Alignment with the Global Biodiversity Framework

Proposals should demonstrate a direct relationship between the selected activities and the gaps identified through the global review of the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework.

The four thematic areas are particularly connected to the following framework goals and targets:

  • Ecosystem restoration and protection: Goal A and Targets 2, 3 and 11;
  • Biodiversity mainstreaming: Targets 14 and 15;
  • Biodiversity finance and resource mobilization: Goal D and Targets 18, 19, 20 and 23; and
  • Genetic resources and digital sequence information: Goal C and Target 13.

Applicants should not merely mention these targets. A strong proposal will explain how project activities, outputs, outcomes and indicators will contribute to the selected framework targets and the beneficiary country’s National Biodiversity Strategy and Action Plan.

The official alignment between the global review gaps and KBF priorities is provided in the KMGBF collective review mapping document.

Project Funding and Duration

The funding ceiling depends on the project’s geographical coverage.

Single-Country Projects

A country-level or subnational project may request no more than US$500,000.

Such projects should concentrate on the implementation of national biodiversity priorities within one beneficiary country. Activities may cover the entire country or selected provinces, districts, landscapes, watersheds, ecosystems or coastal areas.

Multi-Country Projects

A regional project involving more than one country may request up to US$800,000.

A regional proposal should demonstrate genuine cross-border or regional value. Listing several countries without explaining their shared biodiversity problem, coordination arrangements and collective results is unlikely to be sufficient.

Each participating country in a multi-country proposal must provide its own government endorsement letter.

Project Duration

Projects must have an implementation period of at least 12 months and no more than 24 months.

The implementation timetable should be realistic, with sufficient time for:

  1. Project inception and stakeholder consultation;
  2. Baseline assessments;
  3. Technical or policy interventions;
  4. Capacity-building and community participation;
  5. Monitoring of results;
  6. Documentation and communication;
  7. Evaluation and learning; and
  8. Sustainability, replication or handover arrangements.

The official start date will be connected to the transfer of funds by the UN Multi-Partner Trust Fund Office.

Programme Support Costs and Co-Funding

Programme support costs charged by the participating UN organization must not exceed 7%.

The project template contains space to report other sources of finance and co-funding. However, the KBF Operations Manual explains that projects may receive co-funding from UN entities, governments or development partners but does not make co-funding compulsory.

Applicants should distinguish clearly between:

  • The amount requested from the KBF;
  • Confirmed co-financing;
  • In-kind government or partner contributions; and
  • Any parallel financing that supports, but is not managed through, the proposed project.

Institutional Submission Arrangements

Each proposal must be jointly developed by the beneficiary country and a participating United Nations organization selected by the country.

For the 2026 call, KBF resources will be transferred directly only to UN agencies. The beneficiary country accesses the approved resources through the participating UN organization.

National and local government bodies, civil-society organizations, community-based organizations, academic institutions, private-sector organizations and other non-UN entities may be included as implementing partners or sub-partners where appropriate. They cannot independently submit a proposal directly to the Fund under this call.

The proposal template allows up to three participating organizations, although one or two are preferred. When more than one UN organization is involved, the proposal must identify the lead or coordinating organization and clearly explain the responsibilities of each participating organization.

Required Government Endorsement

Every proposal must include an endorsement letter signed by either:

  • The country’s national focal point for the Convention on Biological Diversity; or
  • A designated official in the lead government ministry responsible for the proposal.

Endorsement letters from more than one relevant ministry will be considered an advantage, particularly for projects involving several sectors.

For example, a biodiversity-mainstreaming project involving agriculture, forestry, finance and local government may benefit from demonstrating formal support across the relevant ministries rather than relying on one institution alone.

For a multi-country project, a separate endorsement letter is required from every participating country.

A proposal that does not include the required endorsement will not be evaluated.

Information Required in the Project Proposal

Applicants must use the official KBF proposal template and provide complete information. The required basic information includes:

  • Project title;
  • Primary and secondary thematic areas;
  • A project description of no more than 50 words;
  • Anticipated start date and project duration;
  • Participating UN organizations and their respective roles;
  • Primary and secondary project focal points;
  • Geographic scope;
  • Beneficiary countries and national focal points;
  • Gender Equality Marker;
  • Relevant Sustainable Development Goal targets;
  • Total amount requested;
  • Budget allocation for each participating organization;
  • Sources and value of co-financing, where applicable; and
  • Required institutional signatures.

The official KBF Project Proposal Template requires the following principal sections.

1. Situation Analysis

The situation analysis has a limit of 500 words.

It should provide an evidence-based explanation of the biodiversity problem, its causes, affected ecosystems and communities, current policy or institutional gaps, and opportunities for reversing biodiversity loss.

The analysis should connect the identified problem with the 2050 vision, the four long-term goals of the Global Biodiversity Framework, the 23 targets for 2030 and relevant national biodiversity priorities.

References may be provided through footnotes, which are not counted within the stated word limit.

2. Project Objectives

The objectives section has a limit of 200 words.

Objectives should identify the specific changes the project will produce and explain how those changes will accelerate or expand implementation of the Global Biodiversity Framework.

Objectives should be measurable and achievable within the proposed 12-to-24-month period.

3. Theory of Change

The theory-of-change section has a limit of 500 words.

It should present a logical connection between:

  • Project inputs;
  • Planned activities;
  • Immediate outputs;
  • Medium-term outcomes;
  • Long-term impact;
  • Critical assumptions; and
  • External risks or enabling conditions.

The theory of change should show why the proposed activities are expected to address the identified root causes rather than simply describing a list of activities.

4. Coordination, Complementarity and Added Value

This section has a limit of 400 words.

Applicants should explain how the proposed project will complement previous, ongoing and planned projects in the beneficiary country. The proposal should identify relevant government programmes, UN initiatives, Global Environment Facility projects and other biodiversity investments.

It should also explain how the project team will coordinate with government bodies, UN agencies, development partners, civil society and other stakeholders.

5. Lessons Learned and Innovation

This section has a limit of 200 words.

Applicants should summarize the lessons drawn from comparable initiatives and explain how those lessons have shaped the proposed design.

Innovation may involve new technology, financing arrangements, institutional models, community approaches, policy mechanisms, data systems or scalable conservation techniques. Innovation should solve an identified problem and not be included merely as a promotional claim.

6. Sustainability, Exit Strategy and Replication

This section has a limit of 200 words.

The proposal should explain how results will continue after KBF financing ends. Applicants should address:

  • Environmental sustainability;
  • Institutional ownership;
  • Long-term financial requirements;
  • Government responsibilities;
  • Continued community participation;
  • Handover arrangements;
  • Maintenance of infrastructure or information systems; and
  • Opportunities for replication or expansion.

7. Social Impact

The social-impact section has a limit of 400 words.

It should address gender equality and women’s empowerment, youth participation, vulnerable and marginalized groups, persons with disabilities, and the participation of Indigenous Peoples and Local Communities.

Where Indigenous Peoples or local communities may be affected, the proposal should explain how they participated in project design, how their ownership will be supported and whether free, prior and informed consent procedures are required.

Where relevant social or environmental risks exist, a comprehensive safeguard strategy should be attached.

8. Communications, Outreach and Learning

This section has a limit of 200 words.

Every project is expected to include communication, outreach and learning activities that make results accessible and promote replication.

Applicants should identify:

  • Target audiences;
  • Communication products;
  • Outreach methods;
  • Languages to be used;
  • Knowledge-sharing arrangements; and
  • How project lessons will influence policy or future programming.

9. Detailed Budget

Applicants must use the official budget template. Budgets prepared in a different format may not be considered.

The budget must be organized by outcome, output and activity. Each activity must also be allocated to the appropriate United Nations expenditure category. Activities involving several types of expenditure should be divided accordingly.

The standard categories cover:

  • Staff and other personnel;
  • Supplies, commodities and materials;
  • Equipment, vehicles and furniture;
  • Contractual services;
  • Travel;
  • Transfers to implementing counterparts;
  • General operating and other direct costs; and
  • Indirect programme support costs.

The official KBF Budget Template should be used.

10. Results Framework

The results framework must contain appropriate indicators at both outcome and output levels.

Each indicator should include:

  • A defined baseline;
  • A measurable target;
  • A target date;
  • Means of verification; and
  • The organization responsible for measurement.

Indicators should follow the SMART principles: specific, measurable, achievable, relevant and time-bound.

11. Implementation Workplan

The workplan should organize activities by output and implementation month. It should cover the entire project period and clearly indicate the sequence and timing of major activities.

The workplan should correspond directly with the results framework and budget. An activity appearing in the budget but not in the workplan, or vice versa, may indicate an incomplete project design.

12. Risk-Management Framework

The proposal must identify risks that could prevent the project from achieving its intended results.

The risk assessment should cover:

  • Contextual risks, including political instability, conflict and security;
  • Institutional risks affecting government or partner participation;
  • Programmatic and implementation risks;
  • Environmental and social risks;
  • Economic and financial risks;
  • Safeguarding risks; and
  • Other project-specific risks.

For every material risk, the proposal should describe its likelihood, impact, overall rating, implications, mitigation measures and responsible risk owner.

A separate risk-management plan should be attached when critical or high-level risks require more detailed treatment.

Mandatory and Optional Annexes

The proposal template identifies the following mandatory annexes:

  1. Detailed implementation workplan; and
  2. Results-based budget and budget classified by United Nations expenditure categories.

Depending on the project, applicants may also attach:

  • A more detailed baseline and situation analysis;
  • Maps of the intervention area;
  • Maps for transboundary or multi-country projects;
  • A full theory-of-change diagram;
  • Detailed descriptions of outcomes, outputs and activities;
  • Allocation of responsibilities among implementing partners;
  • A comprehensive safeguard strategy;
  • An Indigenous Peoples and Local Communities engagement plan;
  • A monitoring and evaluation plan; and
  • A stakeholder-engagement plan.

Two Submission Deadlines

The 2026 call uses two submission deadlines.

Stage 1 Deadline: 15 September 2026

Proposals submitted by 23:59 on 15 September 2026 will receive priority review.

The first group of approved projects is expected to be announced and launched during the seventeenth meeting of the Conference of the Parties to the Convention on Biological Diversity.

Stage 2 Deadline: 15 November 2026

Eligible proposals submitted by 23:59 on 15 November 2026 will be reviewed and processed, with results expected to be announced by 31 December 2026.

The official announcement states that all eligible applications will be received and reviewed. Nevertheless, applicants capable of submitting a complete and properly endorsed proposal by the first deadline may benefit from the priority-review timetable.

How to Submit a Proposal

Applications must be emailed directly to the Kunming Biodiversity Fund Secretariat at kbf@un.org.

A complete submission should include:

  1. The completed project proposal template;
  2. The completed project budget template;
  3. A detailed implementation workplan;
  4. The required government endorsement letter or letters;
  5. Any required safeguard or risk-management documents;
  6. Relevant optional annexes;
  7. The names and contact details of the project focal points; and
  8. Any institutional signatures required by the templates.

Applicants should use a clear email subject line identifying the 2026 KBF Call for Proposals, the beneficiary country and the project title.

Files should be clearly named and checked before submission. Applicants should also ensure that attachments are not too large for email delivery.

Review and Selection Process

The KBF Secretariat will initially check whether each proposal satisfies the submission requirements. Proposals that are incomplete, submitted after the relevant deadline or missing the required endorsement may not proceed to technical assessment.

Eligible proposals will be assessed by the KBF Independent Technical Advisory Group. The group will consider the strength, feasibility, sustainability and strategic alignment of each project before recommending a shortlist to the KBF Executive Council.

The linked KBF Operations Manual indicates that technical assessment is likely to consider:

  • Whether the biodiversity problem is clearly defined and urgent;
  • Whether the project presents a credible pathway to transformational impact;
  • The degree of innovation and use of previous lessons;
  • Whether activities logically lead to the proposed results;
  • Evidence that the project was co-created with the beneficiary country;
  • Alignment with the country’s biodiversity implementation strategy;
  • The quality of SMART indicators and the results framework;
  • Communication, outreach and learning arrangements;
  • Integration of gender equality and women’s empowerment;
  • Meaningful engagement of Indigenous Peoples and Local Communities;
  • The quality of the risk-management framework;
  • The practicality of the implementation workplan;
  • The justification and alignment of the proposed budget;
  • Synergies with earlier or ongoing projects; and
  • Potential for sustainability, replication and scale-up.

Applicants may be invited to present their proposal, answer questions or provide further information before a final decision is taken.

The Executive Council may approve a project, approve it subject to recommendations or reject it. Where conditions or recommendations are imposed, the proponent or participating organization may be required to explain within 14 days how those recommendations will be addressed.

The KBF Secretariat will not provide progress updates or feedback while proposals are under review. The nominated project focal point will receive the final decision by email.

Fund Transfer and Project Management

Approved resources will be transferred in tranches.

The first tranche will be released following Executive Council approval of the project document. The KBF Secretariat will prepare the required Fund Transfer Request, after which the UN Multi-Partner Trust Fund Office will process the approved transfer.

The Fund indicates that the transfer should normally be completed within five working days after the UN Multi-Partner Trust Fund Office receives the completed request.

Monitoring, Evaluation and Reporting

The participating UN organization will be responsible for complying with KBF monitoring and evaluation requirements and its own institutional policies and procedures.

The project budget should contain sufficient resources for:

  • Routine monitoring;
  • Biodiversity and socioeconomic data collection;
  • Baseline and end-line measurement;
  • Narrative progress reporting;
  • Financial reporting;
  • Relevant evaluations;
  • Stakeholder learning; and
  • Communication of project results.

The KBF Secretariat may conduct field visits and monitor progress against the approved workplan. Participating organizations may also be required to contribute to KBF learning, evaluation and knowledge-sharing exercises.

How to Develop a Strong Proposal

Prospective project teams should begin with the beneficiary country’s National Biodiversity Strategy and Action Plan rather than starting with a pre-selected activity.

A competitive preparation process should include the following steps:

  1. Identify a specific implementation gap in the national biodiversity strategy.
  2. Connect that gap to the findings of the global review.
  3. Select the most relevant KBF thematic area or areas.
  4. Secure the involvement of a participating UN organization at the beginning of project development.
  5. Consult the relevant government ministry and CBD national focal point.
  6. Engage affected communities, women, youth and other stakeholders during design.
  7. Establish an evidence-based baseline.
  8. Develop a clear theory of change.
  9. Define measurable outcomes, outputs and SMART indicators.
  10. Prepare a realistic 12-to-24-month workplan.
  11. Align every budget item with an activity and expected result.
  12. Explain how the intervention is innovative, sustainable and capable of replication.
  13. Assess environmental, social, institutional and operational risks.
  14. Obtain all endorsement letters and signatures before the deadline.
  15. Conduct a final compliance review against the official guidelines and templates.

Applicants should avoid broad proposals that attempt to address every biodiversity challenge within one project. A focused intervention with clear evidence, ownership and measurable outcomes will generally be more credible than a large collection of loosely connected activities.

Official Application Documents

Applicants should consult and use the following official resources:

  • Official 2026 Call for Proposals
  • Guidelines on the 2026 Full Size Project Application
  • KBF Project Proposal Template
  • KBF Project Budget Template
  • KBF Operations Manual
  • Mapping of KMGBF Global Review Gaps and KBF Priorities

Questions concerning the call may be sent to kbf@un.org.

Conclusion

The Kunming Biodiversity Fund 2026 Call for Proposals offers an important opportunity to convert national and global biodiversity commitments into measurable action. With up to US$500,000 available for a single-country project and up to US$800,000 for a regional multi-country project, the Fund can support targeted interventions in ecosystem restoration, biodiversity mainstreaming, conservation finance and equitable benefit-sharing.

However, successful participation requires more than a promising environmental idea. Proposals must be co-developed with a participating UN organization, formally endorsed by the appropriate government authority, aligned with the beneficiary country’s National Biodiversity Strategy and Action Plan, supported by a credible theory of change, and accompanied by a detailed budget, workplan and results framework.

Prospective project teams should begin institutional coordination immediately, particularly if they intend to meet the priority deadline of 15 September 2026. The final submission deadline is 15 November 2026.

item.content:encoded:
The Government of the Czech Republic has opened applications for its Government Scholarships for Developing Countries for the 2027/2028 academic year, providing eligible international students from selected developing and specific third countries with an opportunity to pursue higher education at public universities in the Czech Republic.

The scholarships are offered as part of the Czech Republic’s Foreign Development Cooperation Programme and are designed to support the education and professional development of nationals from selected countries. Depending on the applicant’s country and chosen programme, the opportunity supports selected follow-up Master’s and Doctoral programmes, with studies available in either Czech or English.

For the 2027/2028 academic year, applications are open from 21 August 2026 until 30 September 2026. Prospective applicants are therefore encouraged to begin preparing their academic documents, motivation letter, tests and other application requirements well before the deadline.

Opportunity Overview

  • Opportunity: Government Scholarships – Developing Countries
  • Host country: Czech Republic
  • Academic year: 2027/2028
  • Study level: Follow-up Master’s and Doctoral studies
  • Study mode: Full-time
  • Study language: Czech and English, depending on the programme and applicant’s country
  • Host institutions: Public higher education institutions in the Czech Republic
  • Application period: 21 August 2026 to 30 September 2026
  • Application deadline: 30 September 2026
  • Programme framework: Czech Republic Foreign Development Cooperation

About the Czech Government Scholarships

The Government of the Czech Republic has a long-standing tradition of providing scholarships to international students from developing countries.

The programme forms part of the country’s international development cooperation efforts and seeks to contribute to the educational and professional development of people from selected developing and specific third countries.

According to the Czech Ministry of Education, Youth and Sports, more than 20,000 foreign nationals have completed studies at Czech universities with support from Government of the Czech Republic scholarships since the late 1950s.

The current scholarship programme is governed by Resolution of the Government of the Czech Republic No. 870 of 27 November 2024 and is implemented through cooperation between the Czech Ministry of Education, Youth and Sports, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and the Ministry of Health.

Applicants should therefore understand that this is not simply a university-specific scholarship. It is a government scholarship programme connected to the Czech Republic’s broader foreign development cooperation policy.

Which Countries Are Eligible for the 2027/2028 Scholarships?

One of the most important aspects of this scholarship is that eligibility is restricted to nationals of specific countries.

For the 2027/2028 academic year, Government of the Czech Republic scholarships are available only to citizens of the following countries:

Europe and Eastern Europe

  • Bosnia and Herzegovina
  • Georgia
  • Ukraine
  • Belarus, specifically democratic forces

Africa

  • Ethiopia
  • Gabon
  • Mauritania
  • Zambia

Asia

  • Bangladesh
  • Cambodia
  • Palestine

Latin America

  • Guatemala
  • Honduras

Applicants should carefully verify their nationality before beginning the application because nationals of countries outside the official eligible-country list cannot apply under this particular scholarship call.

What Study Programmes Are Available?

The Government of the Czech Republic scholarship supports selected full-time programmes rather than every degree programme offered by Czech universities.

The available programmes are divided into studies conducted in Czech and studies conducted in English.

1. Czech-Language Study Programmes

For eligible applicants from Bosnia and Herzegovina, Georgia, Ukraine and Belarus, the scholarship can support selected follow-up Master’s programmes taught in the Czech language.

These programmes generally consist of:

  • A one-year preparatory Czech language course; followed by
  • A two-year follow-up Master’s degree programme in a selected field.

The preparatory language training is part of the scholarship and is provided by the Institute for Language and Preparatory Studies of Charles University.

Applicants interested in Czech-medium studies should consult the official list of selected areas of study before choosing a programme.

2. English-Language Master’s Programmes

Applicants from all countries included in the eligible-country list can apply for selected follow-up Master’s programmes delivered in English.

The English-medium Master’s programmes are generally two years in duration.

However, applicants should not assume that every Master’s degree offered by Czech public universities is covered by the scholarship. Candidates must select a programme from the official list of eligible English-medium programmes published for the scholarship call.

3. English-Language Doctoral Programmes

The scholarship also supports selected Doctoral study programmes taught in English.

These programmes generally last between three and four years, depending on the specific programme.

Doctoral applicants must have already completed a Master’s degree before they can qualify for scholarship support at the doctoral level.

Academic Requirements

Applicants should pay particular attention to the academic qualification requirements because the required previous degree depends on the level of study being pursued.

Requirements for Master’s Applicants

To receive a government scholarship for a follow-up Master’s programme, an applicant must have completed a Bachelor’s degree or equivalent undergraduate study programme.

The Bachelor’s qualification should provide the academic foundation necessary for the selected Master’s programme.

Applicants should also check the admission requirements of their selected university and degree programme because meeting the general government scholarship requirement does not necessarily mean that the applicant automatically meets every university-specific admission requirement.

Requirements for Doctoral Applicants

Applicants seeking a government scholarship for a Doctoral programme must have completed a Master’s degree or equivalent qualification.

Doctoral applicants should pay particular attention to the requirements of their selected doctoral programme, including any academic, research or admission requirements specified by the university.

English Language Requirement

Applicants seeking scholarships for English-medium studies have an additional requirement.

They must complete an online entrance English language test during the scholarship application process.

The purpose of the test is to establish whether the applicant has sufficient command of English for the proposed English-medium studies.

This means prospective applicants should not wait until the final day of the application period to begin completing the online application. The application is not considered complete simply because an applicant has registered.

Applicants should ensure that all mandatory components, including the applicable tests, have been completed.

How the Application Process Works

Applications for the Government of the Czech Republic scholarships are submitted electronically.

The application platform is available through the official Study in Czechia portal under the relevant scholarship call.

Applicants should follow the application process carefully and provide accurate information throughout the registration and submission stages.

Step 1: Confirm Your Eligibility

Before creating an application, determine whether:

  1. You are a citizen of one of the countries listed in the official call.
  2. You are applying for an eligible study programme.
  3. You have the required previous academic qualification.
  4. You meet the requirements for the selected university and programme.
  5. You are not excluded because of your residence or citizenship status.
  6. You can complete the required online tests.
  7. You can submit the complete application before the deadline.

This initial eligibility check can save applicants considerable time.

Step 2: Select an Eligible Study Programme

Applicants should review the official lists of selected programmes before making their academic choice.

The scholarship does not cover every programme available at Czech public universities.

There are separate official lists covering:

  • Selected areas of study for programmes offered in Czech;
  • Selected Master’s programmes offered in English; and
  • Selected Doctoral programmes offered in English.

Applicants should therefore identify an eligible programme rather than selecting a course simply because it is offered by a Czech university.

Step 3: Register on the Application Portal

Applicants must access the relevant scholarship call through the official Study in Czechia portal and register to begin the electronic application.

Each applicant is allowed to register only once and submit only one application.

This makes it particularly important to carefully consider the selected programme and review all information before submitting the application.

Step 4: Complete the Electronic Application Form

Applicants must provide the information requested in the online application form.

The information should be accurate, consistent and supported by the relevant documentation where required.

Candidates should avoid waiting until the final hours before the deadline because technical or connectivity problems can interfere with submission.

Step 5: Write the Motivation Letter

The application is complete only after the applicant has completed the required motivation letter.

The motivation letter should be treated as an important part of the application rather than a formality.

A strong motivation letter should clearly explain the applicant’s:

  • Academic background;
  • Reasons for choosing the proposed programme;
  • Interest in studying in the Czech Republic;
  • Academic and professional objectives;
  • Relevant experience and achievements;
  • Future career plans; and
  • How the proposed education can contribute to the applicant’s professional development and, where appropriate, development in their home country.

Applicants should ensure that their motivation is specific to the chosen field of study rather than submitting a generic scholarship essay.

Step 6: Complete the Mandatory Tests

Applicants must also complete the mandatory tests associated with the scholarship.

Candidates applying for Czech-language studies complete the general study prerequisites test.

Candidates applying for English-medium studies must complete:

  • The general study prerequisites test; and
  • The English language test.

Applicants should therefore allocate sufficient time to complete all mandatory components.

Important Exclusions

The Government of the Czech Republic makes clear that these scholarships are specifically intended to support foreign nationals from developing and specific third countries.

As a result, the following people cannot apply for this particular type of government scholarship:

  • Citizens of the Czech Republic;
  • Citizens of European Union member states; and
  • Other foreign nationals who have a permanent residence permit in the Czech Republic.

Applicants should carefully review their citizenship and residence status before submitting an application.

There is also no legal entitlement to receive a scholarship simply because an applicant submits an application. Meeting the eligibility requirements allows an individual to apply, but it does not guarantee that the scholarship will be awarded.

What Does the Scholarship Cover?

The scholarship is designed to cover the standard length of full-time study under the supported programme.

The exact structure of the scholarship depends on the study pathway.

For eligible Czech-language studies, the support includes the one-year Czech language preparatory course followed by the relevant Master’s programme.

For English-medium studies, the scholarship supports selected two-year Master’s programmes and selected three- to four-year Doctoral programmes.

Applicants should consult the official scholarship guidelines for the detailed financial and administrative conditions applicable to scholarship holders.

Duration of Study

The expected duration depends on the programme selected.

Czech-medium Master’s pathway

  • One year of Czech language preparation
  • Two years of follow-up Master’s study

English-medium Master’s pathway

  • Approximately two years of follow-up Master’s study

English-medium Doctoral pathway

  • Approximately three to four years of Doctoral study

The scholarship is intended to support the standard duration of the relevant full-time study programme.

Application Deadline

The application period for the 2027/2028 Government of the Czech Republic Scholarships for Developing Countries opened on:

21 August 2026

The final application deadline is:

30 September 2026

Applicants must complete and submit the electronic application by 30 September 2026 at the latest.

Successful applicants are expected to begin their studies during the 2027/2028 academic year.

Because the application contains several components, including a motivation letter and mandatory tests, applicants are strongly advised not to leave submission until the deadline.

Official Application Portal

Applications are submitted electronically through the official Study in Czechia portal.

The Government of the Czech Republic scholarship information is also published by the Ministry of Education, Youth and Sports of the Czech Republic.

Prospective applicants should rely on the official scholarship documentation when making decisions about eligibility, study programmes and application requirements.

Important Scholarship Documents

Applicants are encouraged to read the official guidelines carefully before submitting an application.

The Government of the Czech Republic provides detailed guidance covering the terms and conditions of the scholarship.

The official documentation includes:

  • Guidelines for Granting Scholarships of the Government of the Czech Republic – English version
  • Guidelines for Granting Scholarships of the Government of the Czech Republic – Czech version
  • Frequently Asked Questions
  • Lists of selected study programmes
  • Information concerning personal data processing

The official English guidelines are particularly important for international applicants because they explain the applicable rules and conditions in greater detail.

Frequently Asked Questions and Additional Support

Applicants who cannot find answers to their questions in the official scholarship guidelines and FAQ documents can contact the programme support team.

The official information identifies registr@dzs.cz as the contact email for enquiries that are not addressed in the published documentation.

Applicants should first consult the official guidelines and FAQ before contacting the support team, particularly for questions concerning information already explained in the published documents.

Personal Data and Privacy

Applicants should also familiarize themselves with the information concerning the processing and protection of personal data.

The scholarship application involves the collection and processing of personal information, and the Czech authorities provide information about data protection in accordance with applicable European Union data protection requirements.

Applicants should review the relevant privacy information before submitting their applications.

Tips for Preparing a Strong Application

Although meeting the eligibility criteria is essential, applicants should also focus on the quality and completeness of their submission.

1. Start Early

Do not wait until September to begin preparing.

The application involves multiple stages, including registration, programme selection, the motivation letter and mandatory tests.

Starting early gives applicants enough time to identify and correct errors.

2. Choose the Programme Carefully

One of the most important decisions is the selection of the study programme.

Applicants should confirm that their chosen programme appears on the official list of programmes supported by the scholarship.

3. Check Your Academic Qualification

Master’s applicants should confirm that they have completed a Bachelor’s degree.

Doctoral applicants should confirm that they have completed a Master’s degree.

Applicants should also consider whether their academic background aligns with the admission requirements of the programme.

4. Take the English Test Seriously

Applicants applying for English-medium studies must complete the online English language test.

Candidates should prepare for the test and make sure they have adequate time and a suitable internet connection when completing it.

5. Prepare a Targeted Motivation Letter

A generic motivation letter can weaken an otherwise strong application.

The letter should connect the applicant’s academic background, chosen programme and future ambitions.

Applicants should demonstrate why the proposed field of study matters to their professional development and explain why the selected programme is appropriate for their goals.

6. Read the Official Guidelines

Applicants should not rely solely on summaries posted on third-party websites.

The official guidelines contain the authoritative conditions governing the scholarship.

Candidates should read the guidelines before submitting their application and use the FAQ to clarify common questions.

7. Submit Before the Deadline

The deadline is 30 September 2026.

Submitting early reduces the risk of missing the deadline because of technical problems, incomplete tests or other unforeseen circumstances.

Who Should Consider Applying?

This scholarship may be particularly valuable for eligible nationals who want to pursue postgraduate education in Europe but need financial support to access higher education abroad.

Potential applicants include:

  • Recent Bachelor’s graduates from eligible countries seeking Master’s-level study;
  • Professionals with a Bachelor’s degree who want to advance their academic qualifications;
  • Master’s graduates from eligible countries interested in doctoral research;
  • Applicants interested in selected fields offered by Czech public universities;
  • Students interested in studying in English;
  • Eligible applicants from the specified countries interested in learning Czech before pursuing a Czech-medium Master’s degree; and
  • Candidates seeking an internationally oriented academic experience that can support their future professional development.

However, applicants must always confirm that their nationality, academic qualifications and intended programme meet the official requirements.

APPLY HERE

Why This Scholarship Is an Important Opportunity

The Government of the Czech Republic Scholarships provide eligible applicants with an opportunity to access postgraduate education at Czech public higher education institutions under a government-supported international development cooperation programme.

The programme is particularly significant because it combines higher education with the Czech Republic’s broader development cooperation objectives.

For successful candidates, studying at a Czech public university can provide exposure to an international academic environment, advanced knowledge in their selected discipline and an opportunity to develop qualifications that can contribute to their future careers.

The programme’s long history also demonstrates the Czech Republic’s longstanding involvement in supporting international students from developing and specific third countries.

Visit HERE to learn more about the Czech Republic Government Scholarships 2027/2028 for Developing Countries.

Final Checklist Before Applying

Before submitting the application, prospective candidates should make sure they have:

  • Confirmed that their country is on the eligible-country list;
  • Confirmed that their academic qualification meets the requirement;
  • Identified an eligible study programme;
  • Checked the language of instruction;
  • Registered on the official application portal;
  • Completed the electronic application form;
  • Prepared and completed the motivation letter;
  • Completed the required general study prerequisites test;
  • Completed the English language test if applying for English-medium studies;
  • Reviewed the official scholarship guidelines;
  • Consulted the FAQ where necessary;
  • Checked the application for errors and inconsistencies;
  • Submitted only one application; and
  • Submitted the completed application by 30 September 2026.

Conclusion

The Government of the Czech Republic Scholarships for Developing Countries 2027/2028 offer eligible nationals from selected countries an opportunity to pursue supported postgraduate studies at public higher education institutions in the Czech Republic.

The programme covers selected follow-up Master’s and Doctoral programmes, with opportunities available in English and, for applicants from specified countries, in Czech following a preparatory language course.

Eligibility is limited to nationals of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Georgia, Ukraine, Belarus (democratic forces), Ethiopia, Gabon, Mauritania, Zambia, Bangladesh, Cambodia, Palestine, Guatemala and Honduras. Applicants must also satisfy the academic and programme-specific requirements.

For the 2027/2028 academic year, the application period runs from 21 August 2026 to 30 September 2026. Because applicants must complete an electronic application, motivation letter and mandatory tests, prospective candidates should begin the process early and carefully follow the official guidelines.

Applicants should use the official Study in Czechia application platform and consult the Czech Ministry of Education, Youth and Sports for authoritative information before submitting their application.

The most important step is to verify eligibility and select an approved programme before investing significant time in the application. Candidates who meet the requirements should use the available application period to prepare a complete, accurate and compelling submission before the 30 September 2026 deadline.

item.content:encoded:
The African Peer Review Mechanism (APRM) has announced its Third Continental Training on South-South and Triangular Cooperation (SSTrC) for Sustainable Development, a virtual capacity-building programme designed to strengthen African expertise, peer learning and partnerships for sustainable development.

Under the theme “Accelerating the Implementation of Agenda 2063 and the SDGs in a Changing Global Order,” the training will explore how South-South and Triangular Cooperation can be used to advance Africa’s development priorities, strengthen institutional capacity, mobilize resources and support implementation of the African Union Agenda 2063 and the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs).

The third edition is scheduled to start on 1 November 2027 and will be delivered virtually, making it accessible to eligible participants across Africa and to Africans in the diaspora.

APRM Third Continental Training 2027: Programme Overview

The training is being organized as part of APRM’s efforts to strengthen knowledge and practical capacity around South-South and Triangular Cooperation (SSTrC).

South-South Cooperation generally refers to collaboration and knowledge exchange among countries of the Global South, while Triangular Cooperation involves collaboration among developing countries with support from an additional development partner, institution or organization.

The programme recognizes the importance of these approaches in helping African countries and institutions respond to changing global economic, political and development dynamics.

Key programme details

  • Programme: APRM Third Continental Training on South-South and Triangular Cooperation
  • Theme: Accelerating the Implementation of Agenda 2063 and the SDGs in a Changing Global Order
  • Starting date: 1 November 2027
  • Modality: Virtual/Online
  • Organizer: African Peer Review Mechanism (APRM)
  • Focus: South-South and Triangular Cooperation, Agenda 2063, SDGs, development partnerships, financing, knowledge management, youth, gender and inclusive governance
  • Geographic focus: Africa, with participation also identified for Africans in the diaspora

The official APRM announcement does not currently state an application deadline. Therefore, applicants should monitor the official announcement for application procedures, registration details and any future deadline.

What Is South-South and Triangular Cooperation?

South-South and Triangular Cooperation has become an increasingly important mechanism for countries and institutions in the Global South to exchange knowledge, technology, expertise, resources and development solutions.

Rather than relying exclusively on traditional development cooperation models, SSTrC encourages countries and institutions to learn from one another and develop partnerships based on shared experiences and complementary capabilities.

For Africa, this can include cooperation in areas such as:

  • Economic development
  • Education and skills development
  • Healthcare
  • Agriculture and food security
  • Technology and digital transformation
  • Climate action
  • Governance
  • Public-sector reform
  • Youth development
  • Gender equality
  • Infrastructure
  • Trade and investment
  • Sustainable development

The APRM training is therefore designed to help participants understand how these cooperation mechanisms can contribute to Africa’s long-term transformation.

Main Objectives of the APRM Training

The programme has several interconnected objectives.

1. Strengthen capacity for South-South and Triangular Cooperation

Participants will develop a stronger understanding of SSTrC concepts, approaches and practical applications.

This can help professionals and institutions identify opportunities for cooperation, develop partnerships and contribute more effectively to development initiatives.

2. Promote peer learning and exchange of best practices

The training will provide an opportunity for participants to learn from experiences across different African contexts and from other development stakeholders.

Peer learning can help participants identify approaches that can potentially be adapted to their own institutions, countries or communities.

3. Enhance implementation of Agenda 2063 and the SDGs

A major focus of the programme is connecting South-South and Triangular Cooperation with the implementation of Agenda 2063 and the Sustainable Development Goals.

This is particularly important because Africa’s development priorities require coordinated action across governments, civil society, development organizations, academia, communities and the private sector.

4. Foster multi-stakeholder partnerships

The programme also seeks to encourage collaboration between different stakeholders working toward sustainable development.

Participants may gain a better understanding of how governments, development partners, civil society organizations, academia, communities and other actors can work together to advance development priorities.

APRM SSTrC Training Programme Modules

The training consists of five major modules, with a new module on Youth, Gender and Inclusive Governance included in this third edition.

Module I: South-South and Triangular Cooperation in a Changing Global Order

The first module will examine the background and evolution of South-South and Triangular Cooperation within a changing global environment.

Topics include the role and influence of:

  • The G20
  • BRICS and other emerging blocs
  • Global South cooperation
  • Changing international development partnerships
  • New geopolitical and economic dynamics
  • Emerging models of international cooperation

This module is intended to help participants understand the broader environment in which SSTrC operates.

Module II: SSTrC, Agenda 2063 and the SDGs

The second module focuses on the relationship between South-South and Triangular Cooperation and Africa’s development frameworks.

Participants will explore how SSTrC can contribute to:

  • Agenda 2063 implementation
  • SDG implementation
  • National development priorities
  • Regional development
  • Institutional cooperation
  • Knowledge and technology exchange
  • Sustainable development initiatives

This module is particularly relevant for professionals involved in development planning, policy, programme implementation and partnerships.

Module III: Financing the Africa We Want

The third module focuses on financing development through South-South and Triangular Cooperation programmes.

Access to sustainable financing remains a major issue for development initiatives across Africa. The module therefore examines how cooperation mechanisms can contribute to mobilizing resources and supporting development programmes.

Potential areas of interest include:

  • Development financing
  • Partnership financing
  • Resource mobilization
  • Cooperation programmes
  • Financing for Agenda 2063
  • Financing for sustainable development

Module IV: Monitoring, Evaluation and Knowledge Management

The fourth module focuses on monitoring, evaluation and knowledge management in SSTrC.

Effective cooperation requires more than establishing partnerships. Stakeholders must also be able to measure results, document lessons and use evidence to improve future programmes.

Participants will therefore explore the importance of:

  • Monitoring development programmes
  • Evaluating outcomes
  • Measuring impact
  • Documenting lessons learned
  • Managing institutional knowledge
  • Sharing best practices
  • Improving future cooperation initiatives

Module V: Youth, Gender and Inclusive Governance

The fifth module is a new component of the programme.

It focuses on:

  • Youth participation
  • Gender equality
  • Inclusive governance
  • Participation in development processes
  • Representation of diverse groups
  • Community-level development
  • Inclusive approaches to SSTrC

The inclusion of this module recognizes that sustainable development requires meaningful participation from young people, women and other groups that contribute to Africa’s transformation.

Who Can Participate?

The APRM identifies a broad range of potential participants. The programme is not limited to government officials.

Target participants include:

APRM National Structures

Individuals working within or connected to APRM National Structures are among the intended participants.

Youth and Women

The programme specifically identifies youth and women as target participant groups, particularly those involved in development, governance, community initiatives or Agenda 2063-related activities.

Africans in the Diaspora

Africans in the diaspora are also identified as a target group, creating an opportunity for Africans living outside the continent to engage with the programme.

Civil Society and Academia

The programme welcomes participation from people working within:

  • Civil society organizations
  • Universities
  • Research institutions
  • Academic organizations
  • Development-focused networks

Development Partners

Professionals associated with development partners are also among the identified target groups.

Practitioners and Development Stakeholders

Practitioners and stakeholders working on development initiatives can benefit from the programme, particularly those whose work relates to Agenda 2063 and South-South and Triangular Cooperation.

Community Leaders

Community leaders advancing community-level initiatives are also specifically identified.

This makes the programme relevant to individuals working at both institutional and grassroots levels.

Geographic Eligibility: Who Can Apply?

Based on the APRM’s stated target participants, the opportunity is primarily designed for Africans and people working on Africa’s development, including Africans in the diaspora.

The announcement does not provide a specific list of eligible African countries. It identifies Africans in the diaspora as a target group and refers broadly to APRM structures, African development stakeholders, civil society, academia, development partners, practitioners and community leaders.

Therefore, interested applicants should check the official registration or application instructions once released to confirm any specific nationality, residency or institutional requirements.

There is no indication in the announcement that eligibility is restricted by race or ethnicity. The geographic emphasis is on Africa and Africans in the diaspora.

Why This Training Matters

The programme is particularly relevant at a time when African countries are navigating significant changes in the global development and geopolitical environment.

South-South and Triangular Cooperation can provide opportunities for African countries and institutions to:

  • Exchange practical knowledge
  • Share successful development models
  • Build institutional partnerships
  • Mobilize development resources
  • Strengthen technical capacity
  • Support innovation
  • Improve policy implementation
  • Strengthen regional cooperation
  • Advance Agenda 2063
  • Accelerate progress toward the SDGs

For individual participants, the training can also strengthen their understanding of international development cooperation and partnership-building.

Previous Strategic Partners

According to APRM, previous cohorts of the training have involved collaboration with several major institutions and development organizations, including:

  • United Nations organs
  • African Union Commission
  • African Union Development Agency – NEPAD
  • World Food Programme
  • Islamic Development Bank
  • Rwanda Cooperation Initiative
  • Egyptian Agency for Partnership for Development
  • Institute for Global Dialogue

These previous partnerships demonstrate the programme’s connection to a broad development cooperation ecosystem.

Click HERE to read more.

Potential Benefits for Participants

Participants can potentially benefit from the programme through exposure to concepts, practices and networks related to international development cooperation.

Key areas of value include:

Knowledge and skills development

Participants can deepen their understanding of SSTrC and how it can be applied to development initiatives.

Agenda 2063 knowledge

The programme provides an opportunity to better understand the role of cooperation in implementing the African Union’s long-term development vision.

SDG implementation

Participants can strengthen their understanding of how development partnerships can support progress toward the Sustainable Development Goals.

Peer learning

The training creates an opportunity to exchange experiences with other professionals, practitioners, researchers and development stakeholders.

Partnership development

The focus on multi-stakeholder partnerships can help participants understand how to develop and strengthen collaborative development initiatives.

Governance and inclusion

The new youth, gender and inclusive governance module adds an important perspective for participants working on inclusive development.

Why Applicants Should Prepare Early

Although the training is scheduled to begin on 1 November 2027, the official announcement currently does not provide an application deadline.

Potential applicants should therefore begin preparing by:

  1. Reviewing the programme objectives.
  2. Identifying how their current work relates to Agenda 2063.
  3. Understanding South-South and Triangular Cooperation.
  4. Preparing a concise professional profile.
  5. Identifying relevant development or community initiatives they have worked on.
  6. Monitoring APRM announcements for registration information.
  7. Preparing to explain how the training could contribute to their professional or community work.

APPLY HERE

Conclusion

The APRM Third Continental Training on South-South and Triangular Cooperation for Sustainable Development presents an important learning opportunity for African development practitioners, young people, women, civil society actors, academics, community leaders, development partners and Africans in the diaspora.

Beginning on 1 November 2027 and delivered virtually, the programme will explore how South-South and Triangular Cooperation can contribute to the implementation of Agenda 2063 and the SDGs. Its five-module structure covers the changing global order, Agenda 2063 and SDG implementation, development financing, monitoring and knowledge management, as well as the increasingly important areas of youth, gender and inclusive governance.

For professionals and community leaders working to advance sustainable development in Africa, the programme can provide a useful platform for strengthening knowledge, learning from peers and understanding how partnerships can be used to translate development commitments into practical action.

Important: The current official announcement does not state an application deadline, so interested participants should monitor APRM for the release of registration and application details.

Click HERE for more training opportunities.
