SEO Title: Mountains ADAPT Small Grants 2026: Up to US$30,000 for Mountain Community Climate Resilience

Meta Description: Apply for the Mountains ADAPT Small Grants 2026 and receive up to US$30,000 to implement community-led climate adaptation and nature-based solutions in East Africa and the South Caucasus. Deadline: 15 September 2026.

Focus Keywords: Mountains ADAPT Small Grants 2026, UNEP grants 2026, climate adaptation grants, mountain community grants, East Africa climate grants, South Caucasus grants, community-based organization grants, nature-based solutions funding, climate resilience funding

Mountains ADAPT Small Grants 2026

Community-based organizations and other eligible local organizations working with mountain communities in East Africa and the South Caucasus have an opportunity to apply for the Mountains ADAPT Small Grants Project for Mountain Community Resilience.

The initiative, implemented by the United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP), is designed to support locally driven solutions that help mountain communities respond to the impacts of climate change while protecting ecosystems, strengthening livelihoods and improving food security. UNEP describes the project as a small-grants scheme providing funding of up to US$30,000 per project for needs-based, community-led adaptation solutions.

The programme is particularly relevant for organizations that are already working directly with mountain communities and have practical solutions that can address climate-related challenges through ecosystem-based and nature-based approaches.

For the 2026 call, solution proposals must be submitted by 15 September 2026 at 11:59 p.m. East African Time/South Caucasus Time.

What Is the Mountains ADAPT Small Grants Project?

The Mountains ADAPT initiative focuses on strengthening the resilience of communities living in mountain areas that are increasingly exposed to climate change.

Mountain regions face a range of climate-related pressures, including changing rainfall patterns, rising temperatures, loss of snow and ice, water-related challenges and worsening natural hazards. These risks can be intensified by structural challenges such as remoteness, limited investment and inadequate access to resources. UNEP emphasizes that local-level adaptation action is important for implementing broader climate policies and achieving climate goals.

The Mountains ADAPT small-grants approach therefore seeks to place communities at the centre of climate adaptation.

Rather than focusing only on large-scale infrastructure or externally designed interventions, the programme supports community-led solutions that respond to locally identified climate risks and needs.

According to the application form, the initiative is intended to help organizations turn practical ideas into solutions that can preserve or restore ecosystems, strengthen livelihoods, improve food security and safeguard natural resources.

What Funding Is Available?

Successful applicants can receive up to US$30,000 per project.

The funding is intended to support the design and implementation of impactful solutions that respond to climate change impacts affecting mountain communities.

The grant can therefore provide an opportunity for eligible organizations to move beyond identifying a climate problem and actually implement a practical intervention within their communities.

The programme also goes beyond financial assistance.

Successful organizations are expected to receive:

  • Capacity development support
  • Training
  • Support for implementing their proposed solution
  • Opportunities for learning and exchange with other grantees and mountain adaptation stakeholders
  • Support for strengthening locally led adaptation action

UNEP states that successful applicants will receive capacity development and training support from UNEP and regional implementing partners, while cross-sectoral learning and exchange are an integral part of the project.

Who Is the Mountains ADAPT Grant Designed For?

The opportunity is intended for local organizations working with mountain communities, rather than individual applicants applying in their personal capacity.

The official application form specifically identifies eligible applicants as registered local non-profit organizations or enterprises, including civil society organizations, community-based organizations, youth organizations and women’s organizations, provided they can supply supporting documentation.

The organizations should:

  1. Be based in an eligible country in the East African Community or South Caucasus.
  2. Be locally registered and able to provide supporting documentation.
  3. Work with mountain communities.
  4. Have activities connected to climate change adaptation or related community resilience work.
  5. Have a solution addressing a climate-related challenge.
  6. Aim to preserve, restore or improve livelihoods, ecosystems or food security.

This makes the opportunity particularly relevant to community-based organizations, local NGOs, civil society organizations, youth-led organizations, women’s organizations and other locally registered organizations with an established connection to mountain communities.

Which Countries Are Eligible?

The programme covers countries in the East African Community (EAC) and the South Caucasus.

UNEP identifies the programme location as EAC partner states and South Caucasus countries.

East African Community

As of 2026, the EAC has eight Partner States:

  • Burundi
  • Democratic Republic of the Congo
  • Kenya
  • Rwanda
  • Somalia
  • South Sudan
  • Uganda
  • Tanzania

The EAC’s official website confirms these eight countries as its current Partner States.

South Caucasus

The South Caucasus region generally includes:

  • Armenia
  • Azerbaijan
  • Georgia

The Mountains ADAPT application form confirms that applicants must be based in a country of the East African Community or the South Caucasus.

Important: The eligibility requirement is based on the location and status of the applying organization, not on an individual’s nationality or ethnicity.

What Types of Projects Are Encouraged?

The central focus is climate adaptation and mountain community resilience, particularly projects that combine community action with ecosystem protection.

The programme encourages solutions that can address climate-related challenges while also producing benefits for people and the natural environment.

Potential areas include:

1. Nature-Based Solutions

Projects can use ecosystems and natural processes to help communities adapt to climate change.

Examples may include:

  • Ecosystem restoration
  • Restoration of degraded landscapes
  • Protection of natural resources
  • Community-based conservation
  • Restoration of natural water systems

UNEP specifically identifies Nature-based Solutions as a core approach for Mountains ADAPT projects.

2. Climate-Smart Agriculture

Organizations working with mountain farmers can consider approaches that make agricultural systems more resilient to changing climate conditions.

Possible areas include:

  • Climate-resilient agricultural practices
  • Sustainable farming
  • Climate-resilient crops
  • Soil conservation
  • Sustainable land management
  • Improved agricultural productivity under changing climatic conditions

3. Water Management

Water availability is an increasingly important issue for mountain communities.

Potential interventions may include:

  • Water harvesting
  • Water retention
  • Improved water management
  • Community-based water conservation
  • Protection of water resources

UNEP specifically lists water harvesting and retention among examples of possible adaptation solutions.

4. Food Security

Projects can focus on helping communities maintain reliable access to food despite climate-related disruptions.

This could involve approaches that strengthen:

  • Local food production
  • Climate-resilient agriculture
  • Sustainable natural-resource management
  • Food systems
  • Community livelihoods

The official application form explicitly highlights enhancing food security as one of the objectives of eligible solutions.

5. Livelihood Improvement

Climate change can place significant pressure on mountain livelihoods.

Projects may therefore seek to diversify or protect income sources while ensuring that natural resources are not degraded.

The programme is intended to support solutions that preserve, restore or improve livelihoods while strengthening ecosystem resilience.

What Makes a Strong Mountains ADAPT Proposal?

A strong proposal should not simply describe climate change as a general problem.

It should demonstrate a clear connection between:

Climate risk → Community need → Practical solution → Ecosystem protection → Improved resilience → Sustainable livelihoods

Applicants should be able to clearly explain:

  • What climate-related problem affects the target community?
  • Which mountain communities are affected?
  • What is causing or worsening the problem?
  • What solution is being proposed?
  • Why is the solution appropriate for the local context?
  • How will the community participate?
  • How will the project protect or restore ecosystems?
  • How will the intervention improve resilience?
  • How will livelihoods or food security benefit?
  • How will the project be implemented?
  • How will results be measured?
  • How can the solution continue beyond the grant period?

The official UNEP programme page emphasizes that projects should empower local communities, respond to identified climate risks and impacts, align with relevant policies and plans, and integrate Nature-based Solutions.

Why Community-Led Climate Adaptation Matters

Mountain communities are often directly dependent on natural resources for their livelihoods.

Agriculture, water resources, forests, livestock, biodiversity and other ecosystem services can all be affected by climate change.

When these systems become less reliable, communities can experience:

  • Reduced agricultural productivity
  • Water shortages
  • Soil degradation
  • Increased exposure to natural hazards
  • Loss of biodiversity
  • Reduced household income
  • Increased food insecurity
  • Greater pressure on natural resources

This is why locally designed adaptation measures can be particularly valuable.

Communities often possess detailed knowledge of their local ecosystems, livelihoods and environmental changes. A community-led approach can help ensure that interventions respond to actual local priorities rather than applying a one-size-fits-all solution.

UNEP describes small grants as an effective way of responding to local needs and strengthening local capacities, particularly among women, youth and other groups.

Key Benefits of the Mountains ADAPT Small Grants

The opportunity offers several potential benefits to successful organizations.

Financial support

Eligible organizations can receive up to US$30,000 to implement their proposed climate adaptation project.

Capacity development

Successful applicants will receive capacity development and training support from UNEP and regional implementing partners.

Community impact

The programme allows organizations to implement solutions directly within mountain communities and respond to locally identified climate challenges.

Environmental protection

Projects are expected to integrate ecosystem-based and nature-based approaches, linking community resilience with environmental sustainability.

Livelihood improvement

Projects can help communities protect, restore or improve livelihoods affected by climate change.

Food security

Solutions can contribute to more resilient food systems and improved food security.

Knowledge exchange

The programme provides opportunities for cross-sectoral learning and exchange among grantees and other stakeholders working on mountain adaptation.

The Importance of Women, Youth and Inclusive Community Participation

Mountains ADAPT is not only concerned with environmental outcomes.

The programme also emphasizes strengthening capacities among women, youth and other groups, while supporting inclusive approaches to climate adaptation.

For organizations preparing applications, this means it can be useful to demonstrate how the proposed project will involve different groups within the target community.

Applicants should consider questions such as:

  • Who participates in decision-making?
  • Who benefits from the intervention?
  • Are women meaningfully involved?
  • Are young people involved?
  • Are vulnerable or marginalized groups considered?
  • Does the project create opportunities for different community groups?
  • How will community knowledge inform the project?

A strong community-led project should demonstrate not only what will be implemented, but also who will participate and benefit.

What Kind of Organization Should Apply?

This opportunity could be particularly relevant to organizations working in areas such as:

  • Climate change adaptation
  • Environmental conservation
  • Community development
  • Sustainable agriculture
  • Food security
  • Water management
  • Ecosystem restoration
  • Natural resource management
  • Rural development
  • Livelihood development
  • Mountain conservation
  • Disaster risk reduction
  • Women’s empowerment
  • Youth development
  • Community resilience

However, organizations should not apply simply because they work in one of these sectors.

The proposed project needs to have a clear connection to mountain communities and climate change adaptation, and the organization must satisfy the programme’s geographical and registration requirements.

Examples of Relevant Project Concepts

Based on the programme’s stated focus, eligible organizations could potentially develop projects around concepts such as:

Climate-smart farming for mountain communities

A project could help farmers adopt agricultural practices that are better suited to changing rainfall patterns, temperature changes and other climate pressures.

Community water harvesting

An organization could develop or strengthen community-level water harvesting and retention systems to improve water availability and resilience.

Ecosystem restoration

A project could restore degraded mountain ecosystems while creating livelihood or environmental benefits for surrounding communities.

Climate-resilient livelihoods

Organizations could develop approaches that diversify household income while reducing pressure on natural resources.

Community food-security initiatives

Projects could strengthen local food production and improve resilience to climate-related disruptions.

These are examples of the types of approaches that align with the programme’s stated themes; applicants should ensure their actual proposal responds to a clearly identified local climate risk.

Click HERE to read more.

Mountains ADAPT Application Deadline

The deadline for the first call is:

15 September 2026 at 11:59 p.m.

The deadline is specified according to East African Time/South Caucasus Time.

Organizations should avoid waiting until the final day to submit their proposals. The application may require time to gather organizational documentation, develop the project concept and ensure that the proposed solution clearly addresses the eligibility requirements.

APPLY HERE

Where the Mountains ADAPT Programme Operates

The programme operates across the East African Community and South Caucasus.

UNEP identifies its location as EAC Partner States and South Caucasus countries.

The programme is therefore relevant to organizations working in mountain areas across these two regions rather than being a global grant open to organizations from every country.

The EAC currently consists of eight Partner States: Burundi, Democratic Republic of the Congo, Kenya, Rwanda, Somalia, South Sudan, Uganda and Tanzania.

UNEP’s Previous Mountains ADAPT Experience

Mountains ADAPT is not an entirely new concept.

UNEP states that the Mountains ADAPT scheme was pilot tested in EAC and South Caucasus countries in 2025.

The previous work provides examples of the types of community-level interventions that can be supported.

For example, UNEP highlights:

  • Georgia: Installation of hydrometeorological stations in public schools alongside climate change knowledge and disaster preparedness activities.
  • Kenya: Training on climate-smart agriculture and dissemination of climate-resilient crops to Indigenous communities north of Mount Kenya.
  • Burundi: Activities addressing soil erosion and diversification of income sources.
  • Azerbaijan: Revitalization of traditional culture and knowledge through a water mill and improved irrigation for public parks.
  • Tanzania: Strengthening village structures through bamboo seedlings and training on sustainable agricultural practices.

These examples demonstrate the broad range of approaches that can contribute to mountain resilience, from agriculture and water management to ecosystem restoration, local knowledge and community capacity building.

Final Takeaway

The Mountains ADAPT Small Grants 2026 opportunity provides an important funding pathway for locally registered organizations working with mountain communities in the East African Community and South Caucasus.

With funding of up to US$30,000 per project, the programme is designed to help community-based and other eligible local organizations turn climate adaptation ideas into practical interventions. The emphasis is on community-led action, ecosystem-based adaptation, nature-based solutions, resilient livelihoods, food security and environmental protection.

Organizations should focus on developing proposals that are locally relevant, clearly connected to climate risks and capable of producing tangible benefits for both communities and ecosystems.

The deadline is 15 September 2026 at 11:59 p.m. East African Time/South Caucasus Time. Eligible organizations should review the requirements carefully and submit their applications through the official UNEP application platform before the deadline.

item.content:encoded:
The University of Connecticut (UConn) is offering an exciting interdisciplinary PhD student research opportunity for candidates interested in the intersection of political geography, health geography, public policy, population health and spatial data science.

The opportunity is based in the Department of Geography, Sustainability, Community, and Urban Studies (GSCU) and focuses on understanding how laws, public policies and political boundaries in the United States can influence population health and health disparities.

The position is particularly relevant for graduates with backgrounds in geography, political science, public health, social work, data science or related social sciences who want to pursue advanced research using geographic information systems, spatial analysis, statistical methods and large-scale demographic and health datasets.

PhD Research Opportunity at the University of Connecticut

This doctoral opportunity will allow the selected student to investigate the relationship between politics, geography, public policy and population health.

The research will examine how political and administrative structures—including laws, policies and electoral boundaries—can shape health outcomes and contribute to differences in health across populations and places.

The research is interdisciplinary and combines approaches from:

  • Political geography
  • Health geography
  • Spatial data science
  • Public health
  • Political science
  • Demography
  • Geographic Information Systems (GIS)
  • Statistics
  • Public policy
  • Population-health research

The opportunity is therefore suited to candidates who are interested not only in traditional geography research but also in using quantitative and computational methods to understand complex social and health-related questions.

Expected Start Date

The selected PhD student is expected to begin the programme in one of the following periods:

  • Winter/Spring 2027, or
  • Fall 2027

Candidates interested in joining UConn during these admission periods are encouraged to contact the relevant faculty member with their CV and a brief description of their research interests.

What Will the PhD Student Research?

The student will work with a broad range of spatial, political, demographic and health datasets.

The research may involve examining how political boundaries and policy environments interact with population characteristics and health outcomes.

Key data sources and research materials may include:

1. Congressional and Legislative District Maps

The student may work with maps of U.S. congressional and legislative districts, including gerrymandered political boundaries.

This provides an opportunity to investigate how the geographic organization of political representation may intersect with demographic and health patterns.

2. Election and Public Policy Data

Research will also incorporate:

  • Election data
  • Political boundaries
  • Public policy information
  • Legislative information
  • Other political datasets relevant to the research questions

These datasets can be used to examine relationships between political environments, policy decisions and population health.

3. U.S. Census and Federal Datasets

The student will work with U.S. Census data and other federal datasets, providing experience in handling large-scale demographic and socioeconomic information.

This may involve examining variables related to:

  • Population characteristics
  • Geography
  • Socioeconomic conditions
  • Demographic differences
  • Community characteristics
  • Health-related disparities

4. Population Health and Health-Disparity Indicators

Another major component of the research is the use of population-health data and indicators of health disparities.

The student will have an opportunity to investigate how health outcomes differ between populations and geographic areas and how those differences may relate to political, geographic and policy environments.

Spatial Data Science and GIS Research

A major feature of this PhD opportunity is its emphasis on spatial data science.

The successful student will work with geographic and quantitative data and may use methods including:

  • Geographic Information Systems (GIS)
  • Spatial analysis
  • Statistical analysis
  • Data management
  • Data visualization
  • Large-dataset analysis
  • Political and demographic mapping
  • Population-health data analysis
  • Computational approaches to geographic research

Candidates with an interest in developing advanced technical skills in these areas may particularly benefit from the opportunity.

Preferred Qualifications

The opportunity is designed for candidates with relevant graduate-level academic preparation and an interest in interdisciplinary research.

The preferred qualifications include the following.

Master’s Degree

Applicants are preferably expected to have a Master’s degree in Geography or a related discipline.

Relevant related fields may include:

  • Political science
  • Public health
  • Social work
  • Other social sciences
  • Related interdisciplinary fields

The important consideration is that the applicant has an academic or research background that connects meaningfully with the proposed research areas.

Interest in Politics, Policy, Health and Place

Candidates should have a strong interest in the relationship between:

  • U.S. politics
  • Public policy
  • Health
  • Geography
  • Place
  • Population outcomes

This interdisciplinary interest is important because the research sits at the intersection of political and health geography rather than focusing exclusively on one traditional academic discipline.

Experience With U.S. Federal Datasets

Experience working with U.S. federal datasets is listed among the preferred qualifications.

Applicants who have previously worked with large public datasets, demographic information, census data or other government datasets may therefore be well positioned for this research opportunity.

Large-Dataset Management and Analysis

The position also calls for experience managing and analyzing large datasets.

This is particularly relevant because the research combines political, geographic, demographic and health information.

Python and/or R

Basic programming and analytical skills are preferred, particularly experience with:

  • Python
  • R
  • Statistics
  • GIS
  • Data visualization

Applicants do not necessarily need to be advanced programmers based on the information provided, but familiarity with these tools would strengthen their preparation for the research.

Communication Skills

Strong written and oral communication skills are also preferred.

This is important for doctoral research because students are expected to communicate their research findings through academic writing, presentations, collaboration and potentially peer-reviewed publications.

What the Selected PhD Student Can Gain

The doctoral research opportunity offers several academic and professional development opportunities.

1. Develop a Unique Dissertation

The student will have the opportunity to develop an individual dissertation at the intersection of:

  • Political geography
  • Health geography
  • Spatial data science

This provides significant scope for developing an original research question that connects political structures, geographic boundaries and population health.

2. Work With an Interdisciplinary Research Team

The student will become part of a multi-university interdisciplinary research team.

Working across institutions and academic disciplines can provide exposure to different research methodologies, perspectives and areas of expertise.

3. Participate in Team Science

The opportunity emphasizes team science and collaborative research.

Rather than conducting doctoral research entirely independently, the student will have opportunities to contribute to a broader research programme involving multiple researchers and disciplines.

4. Contribute to Peer-Reviewed Publications

The student will have opportunities to contribute to peer-reviewed academic publications.

This can be particularly valuable for candidates who intend to pursue careers in:

  • Academia
  • Research
  • Public policy
  • Government
  • Public health
  • Geographic data science
  • Political research
  • Health research
  • International research organizations

5. Develop Advanced Spatial Data Science Skills

The research environment will provide opportunities to strengthen technical capabilities in:

  • Spatial data analysis
  • GIS
  • Statistical analysis
  • Data visualization
  • Large-scale data management
  • Population-health research
  • Political and demographic analysis

These skills can be transferable beyond academia and are increasingly relevant to research, government, policy and data-driven organizations.

Who Should Consider Applying?

This opportunity may be particularly relevant to graduates and researchers interested in the relationship between politics, geography and health.

Potentially relevant academic backgrounds include:

  • Geography
  • Political geography
  • Health geography
  • Public health
  • Political science
  • Social work
  • Sociology
  • Data science
  • Demography
  • Other related social sciences

Candidates who enjoy combining social science research with quantitative and geospatial methods may find this opportunity particularly suitable.

It may also appeal to applicants who want to investigate how political institutions, public policies and geographic boundaries affect communities and health outcomes.

Research Areas Relevant to the Opportunity

Applicants can demonstrate their fit by showing an interest in research themes such as:

  1. Political geography and health
  2. Geographic inequalities in health
  3. Health disparities
  4. Public policy and population health
  5. Political boundaries and health outcomes
  6. Gerrymandering and geographic inequality
  7. U.S. elections and health
  8. Spatial data science
  9. GIS and population-health research
  10. Census and demographic analysis
  11. Geographic patterns of health disparities
  12. Policy-driven differences in community health

The source does not state that applicants must propose a specific dissertation topic in advance, so interested candidates should focus their initial communication on their research interests and relevant academic or technical experience.

How to Express Interest

Interested candidates are instructed to send:

  • A CV
  • A brief description of their research interests

These materials should be sent to:

Debs Ghosh
University of Connecticut
Department of Geography, Sustainability, Community, and Urban Studies

Email: debarchana.ghosh@uconn.edu

Applicants should use their initial communication to clearly demonstrate how their academic background, research interests, technical skills and professional goals connect with the PhD research opportunity.

What Applicants Should Highlight in Their CV and Research Statement

Although the source only specifically requests a CV and a brief description of research interests, applicants can make their materials more relevant by clearly presenting experience related to the advertised research.

Academic background

Highlight relevant degrees, coursework and research experience in areas such as geography, public health, political science, social science or related disciplines.

Quantitative and technical skills

Where applicable, clearly identify experience with:

  • Python
  • R
  • GIS
  • Spatial analysis
  • Statistics
  • Data visualization
  • Data management

Research experience

Include relevant:

  • Research projects
  • Dissertations or theses
  • Publications
  • Conference presentations
  • Research assistantships
  • Data-analysis projects

Relevant datasets

If applicable, mention previous experience working with:

  • Census datasets
  • Federal datasets
  • Health datasets
  • Demographic datasets
  • Election datasets
  • Geographic datasets

Interdisciplinary interests

The opportunity is explicitly interdisciplinary, so applicants should explain how their interests connect different fields rather than presenting their background as belonging to only one academic area.

Click HERE to read more and apply.

Application Deadline

No application deadline is provided in the supplied opportunity announcement.

The announcement identifies the anticipated start dates as Winter/Spring 2027 or Fall 2027, but it does not specify a closing date for expressions of interest.

Therefore, prospective applicants should not assume a deadline that is not stated in the original information. Interested candidates should contact Debs Ghosh for current application and admissions information.

Conclusion

The University of Connecticut PhD student opportunity offers an interdisciplinary pathway for researchers interested in understanding how political systems, public policies, geographic boundaries and population health intersect.

By combining political geography, health geography and spatial data science, the research provides an opportunity to investigate important questions surrounding health disparities and the geographic consequences of political and policy decisions.

The selected student will have opportunities to develop an original dissertation, work with a multi-university research team, participate in collaborative team science, contribute to peer-reviewed publications and strengthen advanced skills in GIS, spatial analysis, statistics, data visualization and population-health research.

For candidates with a relevant Master’s degree and a strong interest in politics, public policy, geography, health and data-driven research, this could be a valuable doctoral research opportunity beginning in Winter/Spring 2027 or Fall 2027. Since no application deadline is included in the supplied announcement, interested candidates should contact Debs Ghosh at debarchana.ghosh@uconn.edu with their CV and a brief description of their research interests.

Click HERE to read more research opportunities.

item.content:encoded:
The Global South Civil Society Microgrants 2026 provide an opportunity for grassroots organizations, civil society groups, youth movements, community-led initiatives, civic coalitions, artists, and other community-focused groups in the Global South to receive funding for projects that strengthen civic engagement and public understanding of critical environmental and climate issues.

The microgrant program, offered by the Pulitzer Center, provides grants ranging from USD 2,000 to USD 4,000 to support projects that meaningfully use Pulitzer Center-supported journalism to engage communities, amplify affected voices, encourage informed dialogue, and equip people with knowledge that can contribute to action at the local, national, regional, or global level.

The 2026 Global South Civil Society Microgrants focus particularly on the interconnected challenges surrounding rainforests, the ocean, and climate and labor. The initiative is designed not simply to fund information campaigns, but to help communities transform high-quality journalism into meaningful civic engagement, public dialogue, creative expression, knowledge sharing, and community action.

The application window for this cycle runs from August 15 to September 6, 2026, making September 6, 2026 the application deadline.

Opportunity Overview

  • Opportunity: Global South Civil Society Microgrants 2026
  • Organization: Pulitzer Center
  • Opportunity type: Grant
  • Grant amount: USD 2,000–4,000
  • Target region: Global South
  • Key regions highlighted: Africa, Latin America, and Southeast Asia
  • Main focus: Climate and environmental civic engagement
  • Priority themes: Rainforest, Ocean, and Climate and Labor
  • Maximum implementation period: Six months
  • Implementation period: October 2026–March 2027
  • Application period: August 15–September 6, 2026
  • Deadline: September 6, 2026
  • Selection announcement: Mid-September 2026
  • Onboarding: October 2026
  • Virtual check-in: December 2026
  • Project closure and reporting: Early March 2027

The Pulitzer Center describes the initiative as a way to support civil society in Global South regions, including grassroots collectives, community-led movements, artists, and civic coalitions, in using Pulitzer Center-supported journalism to contribute to more informed and empowered communities.

What Is the Global South Civil Society Microgrants Program?

The Global South Civil Society Microgrants are designed around the idea that journalism can have an impact beyond publication.

Investigative and explanatory journalism can uncover environmental degradation, expose systemic challenges, document the experiences of affected communities, and provide evidence that helps citizens understand complicated issues. However, communities often need additional opportunities to discuss, interpret, share, and act on that information.

This microgrant program therefore connects journalism with civic engagement.

Rather than funding conventional journalism reporting, the program supports organizations and groups that can take Pulitzer Center-supported journalism and incorporate it into activities that help communities:

  1. Better understand important issues.
  2. Think critically about information and evidence.
  3. Hear perspectives that are often underrepresented.
  4. Engage in meaningful public dialogue.
  5. Connect evidence from journalism to community experiences.
  6. Identify practical responses to local challenges.
  7. Participate more effectively in civic processes.
  8. Contribute to better-informed decisions, practices, and policies.

The Pulitzer Center has worked on climate and environmental issues since its founding in 2006 and supports journalism and engagement initiatives intended to connect reporting with communities and diverse civic actors.

How Much Funding Is Available?

Successful applicants can receive between:

USD 2,000 and USD 4,000

Applicants are expected to clearly state the amount requested and provide a draft budget showing how the funds will be used.

The grant can be used to support either:

  • An existing civic engagement activity that needs additional resources; or
  • A new project that an organization or community group wants to launch.

This makes the opportunity potentially suitable for organizations that already have community engagement programs as well as groups developing a new initiative around one of the program’s priority environmental themes.

Importantly, the proposal should demonstrate a clear connection between the requested funding, the proposed activities, the target audience, and the expected short-term impact.

What Issues Does the Grant Support?

The 2026 Global South Civil Society Microgrants focus on three major areas:

1. Rainforest, Governance and Communities

The rainforest theme examines the factors contributing to the degradation of rainforest ecosystems and the implications for the people and communities whose lives are closely connected to forests.

Projects may explore issues such as:

  • Rainforest degradation
  • Global markets and rainforest destruction
  • The role of finance in environmental degradation
  • Environmental policies
  • Forest governance
  • Indigenous rights
  • Community rights
  • The role of Indigenous peoples in protecting forests
  • The relationship between communities and forest ecosystems
  • The social consequences of rainforest degradation

A strong project under this theme could use Pulitzer Center-supported rainforest reporting to help affected communities better understand the forces driving environmental change and create spaces where community members can discuss possible responses.

The emphasis is not simply on communicating that rainforest degradation exists. Applicants should demonstrate how journalism can be transformed into meaningful engagement with a defined audience.

2. Ocean Health and the Climate Crisis

The second focus area concerns the health of marine environments and the relationship between oceans and climate change.

Potential areas of engagement include:

  • Ocean health
  • Marine environmental degradation
  • Climate change and oceans
  • Ocean governance
  • Marine communities
  • Coastal communities
  • Science-backed solutions
  • Community-led environmental solutions
  • The social and economic consequences of environmental degradation

Projects could, for example, use relevant Pulitzer Center reporting to facilitate community discussions, educational activities, public forums, creative campaigns, or other forms of engagement that help communities better understand marine environmental challenges.

The program is particularly interested in projects that do more than simply distribute information. The reporting should become a meaningful component of the civic engagement process.

3. Climate and Labor

The third priority area focuses on the relationship between climate change and people’s working lives and livelihoods.

Potential issues include:

  • Climate resilience
  • Gender and climate change
  • Livelihoods
  • Adaptation
  • Workers and climate change
  • Community resilience
  • The social effects of environmental change
  • Economic adaptation
  • Vulnerable communities
  • The intersection of climate change and labor

This theme recognizes that climate change affects communities not only through environmental impacts but also through employment, income, livelihoods, working conditions, migration, gender dynamics, and the ability of communities to adapt.

Projects addressing this theme should demonstrate a clear understanding of the community or audience being engaged and explain how Pulitzer Center-supported reporting can help address information gaps or encourage informed discussion.

What Types of Projects Can Be Funded?

The microgrant is deliberately flexible regarding the format of projects.

However, every proposed activity must use at least one published Pulitzer Center-supported journalism project meaningfully as part of the initiative.

Projects should contribute to one or more of the following objectives:

  • Improving community awareness and critical thinking.
  • Encouraging more informed and transparent dialogue.
  • Supporting better-informed decisions, practices, or policies.
  • Representing and amplifying diverse perspectives.
  • Giving affected communities greater visibility.
  • Equipping communities with information that can support action.

Community Engagement

Community engagement projects can connect journalism with specific audiences and communities.

Examples may include:

  • Community learning sessions
  • Knowledge-sharing activities
  • Community organizing
  • Educational discussions
  • Workshops
  • Community forums
  • Small-group discussions
  • Information-sharing initiatives

The objective is to use journalism to help audiences understand underreported issues and identify ways in which they can respond.

Creative Expressions

Creative approaches are also encouraged.

A project could potentially use:

  • Digital campaigns
  • Public performances
  • Creative publications
  • Art-based activities
  • Storytelling
  • Multimedia campaigns
  • Other locally relevant creative formats

Creative projects should still have a clear civic engagement purpose and should meaningfully incorporate Pulitzer Center-supported reporting.

Public Dialogues

Applicants can also propose public dialogue initiatives that bring different stakeholders together.

Potential participants could include:

  • Community members
  • Journalists
  • Researchers
  • Academics
  • Decision-makers
  • Civil society organizations
  • Environmental advocates
  • Youth representatives
  • Other affected stakeholders

The goal should be to create meaningful opportunities for people to engage with evidence, perspectives, and experiences surrounding the selected issue.

Other Innovative Projects

The program also allows applicants to propose innovative approaches that build on existing local cultural practices and creative expressions.

This flexibility means organizations do not necessarily need to replicate conventional workshops or conferences. A strong proposal could use an approach that is culturally appropriate and familiar to the community while still meeting the grant’s civic engagement objectives.

What Makes a Strong Project Proposal?

A competitive proposal should establish a clear connection between the journalism, the issue, the audience, the activities, and the expected impact.

Applicants should avoid presenting a broad environmental project without explaining how Pulitzer Center-supported reporting will be central to the work.

The proposal should answer several important questions.

1. What problem are you addressing?

Clearly explain the environmental or climate-related challenge.

For example:

  • What is happening?
  • Who is affected?
  • Why does the issue matter?
  • What information is missing?
  • Why is the proposed intervention necessary?

2. Who is your target audience?

The proposal should identify a specific audience rather than simply referring to “the public.”

The target audience could be a particular community, youth group, workers, environmental stakeholders, Indigenous community, coastal population, local civic actors, or another clearly defined group.

3. How is the community involved?

Applicants should explain how the people being engaged are involved in designing the project.

This is particularly important when working with communities directly affected by environmental or climate issues.

4. What information gap exists?

Applicants should identify what their audience does not currently understand.

This could involve:

  • Limited access to reliable information
  • Misunderstanding of climate risks
  • Lack of awareness about environmental governance
  • Limited knowledge of community rights
  • Insufficient understanding of scientific evidence
  • Lack of awareness about available solutions

5. How will journalism help address the problem?

The proposal should identify the Pulitzer Center-supported reporting that will be used and explain why it is relevant to the proposed activity.

This is one of the most important aspects of the application.

Selection Criteria

The Pulitzer Center identifies three principal characteristics for projects supported through the microgrant.

Journalism-Inspired

The proposed project must use at least one Pulitzer Center-supported reporting project meaningfully and/or involve a journalist supported by the Pulitzer Center as a central component of the initiative.

This requirement distinguishes the microgrant from a general environmental or community development grant.

The proposal therefore needs to show that journalism is an integral part of the project’s design rather than an unrelated reference.

Audience-Centric

The project must have a clearly defined target audience.

Applicants should explain:

  • Who the audience is.
  • Why the issue matters to them.
  • What information they currently lack.
  • How they will participate.
  • What the project expects them to understand or do as a result.

Impact-Focused

The project should be designed to produce short-term outcomes for its key audiences.

Applicants should therefore think beyond activities.

For example, instead of simply stating that the project will organize three workshops, the proposal should explain what participants are expected to learn, understand, discuss, develop, or change as a result of those workshops.

Projects That Are Not Eligible

Not every environmental or civic project qualifies.

Applicants should carefully distinguish this opportunity from journalism funding, political advocacy, or commercial activities.

The following types of projects fall outside the scope of the grant:

Journalism Projects

The microgrant does not fund journalism or reporting projects.

Applicants seeking funding specifically to conduct reporting should explore the Pulitzer Center’s separate reporting grants and fellowship opportunities.

Projects Without Pulitzer Center-Supported Reporting

A proposal that does not utilize Pulitzer Center-supported journalism does not meet the central requirement of this microgrant.

Direct Advocacy or Lobbying

Projects involving direct advocacy or lobbying, including participation in congressional or parliamentary meetings, are outside the grant’s scope.

Political Candidate or Party Campaigns

Campaigns that involve or indirectly endorse political candidates or political parties are not eligible.

For-Profit Projects

The microgrant is intended to support civic engagement and community-focused initiatives rather than projects primarily designed for profit.

Who Can Apply?

The opportunity is designed for organizations and groups operating in the Global South.

Eligible applicant categories include:

  • Grassroots organizations
  • Community educators
  • Civil society organizations
  • Civil society coalitions
  • Youth movements
  • Community-led groups
  • Other groups working at the intersection of journalism, civic rights, and active citizenship

Applicants should have previous experience developing and implementing civic engagement activities in Global South regions, particularly Africa, Latin America, and Southeast Asia.

Experience With the Relevant Issues

Applicants should demonstrate experience working on the selected topic.

For example, an organization proposing a rainforest project should ideally be able to demonstrate relevant experience with environmental protection, forest communities, Indigenous rights, civic engagement, conservation, climate communication, or related areas.

Similarly, applicants proposing an ocean-focused project should demonstrate appropriate experience with marine environments, coastal communities, ocean governance, climate issues, conservation, or related areas.

Collaboration Capacity

Applicants should also demonstrate a history of working collaboratively with communities or other organizations.

The Pulitzer Center expects partners to have the operational capacity to manage microgrant resources received from an international organization.

This means applicants should be able to demonstrate that they can:

  • Manage project resources responsibly.
  • Implement activities according to the agreed plan.
  • Collaborate with relevant stakeholders.
  • Monitor project progress.
  • Document outcomes.
  • Complete the required reporting.

Geographic Eligibility

The microgrant specifically targets the Global South, with the call highlighting Africa, Latin America, and Southeast Asia.

This makes the opportunity particularly relevant to civil society organizations and community groups operating in African countries, Latin American countries, and countries across Southeast Asia.

The opportunity is not designed for organizations based in the United States. The Pulitzer Center directs U.S.-based applicants to its separate U.S. Civil Society Microgrant program.

Are Individuals Eligible?

The call is structured around organizations, groups, movements, coalitions, and other civil society actors rather than individual applicants seeking personal funding.

The application requirements also ask for the CV of the lead applicant together with a recommendation letter from a department head or organizational/workplace director. This indicates that an individual may serve as the lead applicant or project representative, but the project itself should be connected to an eligible organization or group with the required experience and capacity.

Applicants should therefore ensure that their organizational or group structure and previous civic engagement experience are clearly demonstrated in the application.

Project Duration

The maximum implementation period is six months.

The overall schedule provided for this cycle places implementation between October 2026 and March 2027, following the selection and onboarding stages.

The broader timeline is:

  1. Application period: August 15–September 6, 2026
  2. Selection and announcement: Mid-September 2026
  3. Onboarding meeting: October 2026
  4. Project implementation: October 2026–March 2027
  5. Virtual check-in: December 2026
  6. Project closure and reporting: Early March 2027

Formal project start and end dates will be established in the agreement between the selected partner and the Pulitzer Center.

Financial and Reporting Requirements

Applicants must provide a proposed budget explaining how the requested funding will be spent.

The requested amount should fall within the available range of USD 2,000 to USD 4,000.

At the conclusion of the grant period, selected partners will be expected to submit:

  • A financial narrative report.
  • Information on the activities implemented.
  • Outcomes achieved.
  • Other relevant project results.

Partners are not required to collect detailed financial receipts according to the published grant information.

This does not mean applicants should approach the budget casually. A clear, realistic, and defensible budget can demonstrate that the organization understands how to translate limited resources into meaningful community impact.

What Documents Are Required?

Applicants should prepare the required application materials before submitting the proposal.

The application requires:

1. Project Description

A general description of the proposed project of no more than 400 words.

This section should explain the core idea clearly and concisely.

2. Target Audience and Desired Impact

Applicants must describe who they intend to reach and what they want to achieve.

The application should demonstrate a clear connection between the target audience and the selected issue.

3. Strategy or Methodology

Applicants must explain how they intend to implement the project successfully.

The methodology should describe the main activities, engagement approach, and mechanisms through which the project will achieve its intended results.

4. Implementation Timeline

The proposal should include a practical timeline showing when major activities will take place.

5. Project Budget

Applicants should provide the amount requested and a draft budget showing how the funds will be allocated.

6. Consent From Indigenous or Traditional Community Members

If the proposed project includes knowledge exchange activities involving Indigenous peoples or traditional communities, applicants must provide a statement from a community member demonstrating consent.

This can be submitted as:

  • A signed letter; or
  • A recorded message.

This requirement is particularly important for projects working directly with Indigenous or traditional communities and reinforces the importance of meaningful community participation and consent.

7. Lead Applicant’s CV and Recommendation Letter

Applicants must provide a copy of the CV of the lead applicant only.

The CV should be accompanied by a recommendation letter from an appropriate authority, such as:

  • A department head; or
  • The director of the applicant’s organization or workplace.

Important Questions to Consider Before Applying

The Pulitzer Center encourages applicants to think carefully about several questions when developing their proposals.

How has the selected issue affected your target group?

Do not simply describe the global climate or environmental problem. Explain its local consequences.

How will you engage the community?

Explain the specific engagement methods you intend to use.

More importantly, demonstrate that the community is not merely a passive audience but has been considered in the design of the project.

What information gaps exist?

Identify the knowledge or information challenges that prevent the target group from fully understanding the issue.

What format will you use?

Explain whether your project will use:

  • Community discussions
  • Digital campaigns
  • Public dialogues
  • Creative performances
  • Educational sessions
  • Knowledge-sharing events
  • Publications
  • Other innovative approaches

Have you implemented similar work before?

Previous experience can help demonstrate that the organization has the capacity to deliver the proposed project.

How does the Pulitzer Center reporting support the project?

This is perhaps the most important question.

Applicants should clearly identify the relevant Pulitzer Center-supported journalism and explain how the reporting will be incorporated into the project’s activities and desired outcomes.

How to Make Your Application Stronger

Although funding is relatively small, the competition for grants can still be significant. Applicants should therefore focus on clarity, relevance, feasibility, and measurable impact.

Select a Specific Problem

Avoid proposals that attempt to address every aspect of climate change.

Instead, identify a specific issue affecting a clearly defined community.

Choose the Right Journalism

The Pulitzer Center-supported reporting should be closely connected to the proposed project.

Do not select a story simply because it is related to climate change. Explain how the story provides evidence, perspectives, or information that can help your target audience understand its own circumstances.

Define Your Audience

A proposal aimed at “everyone” is usually less compelling than one designed around a specific audience.

Clearly explain who will participate and why they are the right audience.

Demonstrate Community Participation

Where possible, show that community members have been consulted or included in the project’s development.

This is especially important for initiatives involving Indigenous peoples and traditional communities.

Build a Realistic Budget

The budget should correspond directly to the proposed activities.

Every major expenditure should have a clear connection to implementation.

Focus on Outcomes

Think about what will be different after the project.

For example, participants might:

  • Gain a better understanding of a climate issue.
  • Develop greater awareness of environmental governance.
  • Access information they previously lacked.
  • Engage in informed public dialogue.
  • Develop community responses.
  • Connect with journalists or decision-makers.
  • Become better equipped to take local action.

Application Deadline

The application period for the 2026 Global South Civil Society Microgrants is:

August 15–September 6, 2026

Therefore, the deadline is September 6, 2026.

Applicants should avoid waiting until the final day to prepare their proposal, particularly because the application requires a project description, methodology, budget, timeline, lead applicant CV, recommendation letter, and potentially a community consent statement.

How to Apply

Interested organizations should review the official Global South Civil Society Microgrants opportunity page on the Pulitzer Center website and complete the application through the designated application process. The official opportunity page currently provides application options in multiple languages, including English, Spanish, Portuguese, French, and Indonesian.

Before submitting, applicants should ensure that:

  • The organization is based in an eligible Global South region.
  • The project addresses one of the three priority themes.
  • At least one published Pulitzer Center-supported journalism project is meaningfully incorporated.
  • The target audience is clearly identified.
  • The expected impact is clearly explained.
  • The project methodology is realistic.
  • The implementation timeline is feasible.
  • The requested amount is between USD 2,000 and USD 4,000.
  • The draft budget is complete.
  • The lead applicant’s CV is included.
  • The required recommendation letter is included.
  • Community consent documentation is included where applicable.
  • The proposal is submitted before September 6, 2026.

APPLY HERE

Why This Grant Is Important

The Global South Civil Society Microgrants are particularly significant because they recognize that environmental challenges cannot be addressed through journalism, policy, or activism alone.

Communities need access to reliable information, opportunities to interpret that information within their own circumstances, and platforms where different stakeholders can engage with one another.

By connecting Pulitzer Center-supported journalism with grassroots civic engagement, the program creates an opportunity for organizations to transform reporting into practical community experiences.

For example, journalism documenting rainforest degradation can become the basis for community discussions about forest governance. Reporting on ocean health can inform conversations among coastal communities about environmental risks and solutions. Reporting on climate and labor can help workers and communities explore how climate change affects livelihoods, gender, adaptation, and resilience.

The strongest projects will therefore likely be those that can demonstrate a clear pathway from journalism to understanding, from understanding to dialogue, and from dialogue to meaningful community engagement.

Visit HERE to learn more about the Global South Civil Society Microgrants 2026.

Conclusion

The Global South Civil Society Microgrants 2026 offer grassroots and civil society organizations an opportunity to secure USD 2,000–4,000 to develop or strengthen civic engagement projects addressing some of the most pressing environmental and climate challenges facing communities today.

With a focus on rainforests, ocean health, and climate and labor, the program is especially relevant to organizations working with communities affected by environmental degradation, climate change, livelihood challenges, and related social and governance issues.

However, applicants should remember that this is not a conventional environmental grant and not a journalism reporting grant. The central requirement is to use Pulitzer Center-supported journalism as a meaningful component of civic engagement. Successful proposals should clearly identify their target audience, demonstrate relevant organizational experience, explain the information gap they intend to address, present a practical engagement strategy, and show how the project can generate short-term impact.

Organizations across Africa, Latin America, and Southeast Asia with relevant civic engagement experience should consider this opportunity carefully, particularly if they already work with communities on climate, environmental justice, Indigenous rights, livelihoods, ocean conservation, rainforest protection, or related issues.

With the application deadline set for September 6, 2026, eligible organizations should begin preparing their project concept, identifying relevant Pulitzer Center-supported reporting, developing their budget and timeline, and gathering the required supporting documents as early as possible.
